reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: The affected hand performs complex, apparently purposeful movements outside the patient's voluntary control, and is felt as foreign or not their own
Patients often personify the limb and may use the other hand to restrain it
The callosal (anterior) form typically causes intermanual conflict, where one hand opposes the actions of the other
The frontal (medial) form, associated with anterior cerebral artery territory and supplementary motor area lesions, produces compulsive grasping and groping in the dominant hand
A posterior (parietal) variant is linked with more withdrawal-type or levitating movements and sensory features
Causes include stroke, corticobasal degeneration, tumour, trauma, and callosal surgery
Management is supportive, addressing the underlying disorder, with behavioural strategies to occupy or constrain the limb
reference.pathophysiology: Alien hand syndrome reflects a disconnection between the systems that generate movement and those that experience movement as self-willed. In the callosal form, damage to the corpus callosum impairs interhemispheric communication, so the non-dominant hemisphere can drive the hand independently, producing intermanual conflict. In the frontal form, medial frontal lesions involving the supplementary motor area and anterior cingulate release environmentally triggered grasping and reaching behaviours from voluntary inhibitory control. Parietal lesions disrupt the sense of ownership and agency over the limb. In each case, motor acts are produced without the normal accompanying sense of intention, so the hand feels autonomous and alien.
additionalDifferentials: Anterior or middle cerebral artery stroke
Corpus callosum lesion or surgical callosotomy
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain to identify callosal, frontal, or parietal lesions
Neuropsychological assessment of interhemispheric function and apraxia
Investigations for corticobasal degeneration and other neurodegenerative disease
Electroencephalography and cerebrospinal fluid studies where prion disease is suspected
redFlags: Acute onset indicating a new stroke
Rapidly progressive cognitive and motor decline suggesting a neurodegenerative or prion disorder
Movements causing self-injury or endangering the patient
New focal neurological signs pointing to an expanding lesion
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the cause; the alien hand from stroke may partially improve, whereas that due to corticobasal degeneration or prion disease progresses with the underlying illness, and the phenomenon can be persistently disabling.
pitfalls: Dismissing the complaint as functional or psychiatric without imaging
Failing to recognise corticobasal degeneration as an underlying cause
Overlooking safety risks from uncontrolled limb movements
Confusing the different anatomical subtypes and their localisation
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Treat the underlying cause — stroke, tumour, corticobasal degeneration or other neurodegeneration — as the primary determinant of outcome
Use occupational and behavioural strategies, including keeping the affected hand occupied with an object or task to reduce involuntary interference
Apply sensory cueing, mirror and visuospatial techniques to reduce intermanual conflict
Address safety by removing hazards the autonomous hand might grasp and supporting activities of daily living
Manage associated focal dystonic posturing with botulinum toxin where present
Provide neuropsychological support and educate patient and carers about the involuntary, non-volitional nature of the movements
Refer to neurology and neurorehabilitation, with palliative and supportive care where the cause is progressive
